news_title: Are recalls really up 400 percent?
efet_title: Are recalls really up 400 percent?
efet_body:
After the "Summer of Recalls," many consumers are understandably nervous about food safety, wondering if the industry is doing enough to protect them. Headlines claiming that recalls are up 400 percent this year fueled consumer fear, and the public is now looking for reassurance about the safety of our food supply.
It’s a given that public health must be the highest priority for the food industry. It’s also important to understand the reality we live in today, where the viral nature of information causes claims to spread quickly and widely, without much regard to their accuracy or context. The 400 percent statistic wasn’t necessarily incorrect, but understanding the specific numbers it was representing will help offset consumer fear — without detracting from the responsibility the food industry has to keep consumers safe.
So let me clarify what the number is measuring, what that means for how you shop, and what you can expect from the industry so you can respond to a recall correctly.
Frequency vs. Scale
First, the
400 percent figure spread through social media
, not a published report. A social media creator claimed she had read “something” that said recalls were up 400 percent, but didn’t point to where the number had come from or what it was specifically representing. The 400 percent story moved fast because it confirmed what people already felt about recalls happening more frequently.
The
underlying data
tells a different story. The number of recalls hasn’t changed much: regulators recorded 1,634 recalls in the first half of 2026, compared to 1,636 during the same period last year. However, recalls are getting bigger and more complex. Recalled units went from 211.2 million to 941.2 million year over year, which is where the 400 percent comes from.
Complex, global supply chains can cause a single issue to impact dozens of brands at once because they share a supplier. Case in point:
lettuce
contaminated with Cyclospora came from an international supplier with wide distribution. This supplier distributed tainted lettuce that ended up in numerous Taco Bell restaurant locations, plus multiple grocery store brands nationwide. When a small number of large suppliers serve many brands, one contamination event can have a much wider footprint than it did a decade ago.
Frequency and scale are two different problems with two different solutions. If recalls were happening more frequently, we’d need to be looking at prevention protocols and food safety culture. Larger scale recalls suggest that we need to be looking at traceability systems and consumer communication practices, so we can quickly identify affected product and get that information into the hands of people at risk. Both are areas that the industry is making progress in, and both still have a lot of work that needs to be done.
What does this mean for consumers?
A large recall doesn’t automatically mean the food supply is unsafe. It may simply be that one ingredient traveled more widely than it used to, the way Cyclospora-contaminated
lettuce
did this summer. Consumers don’t have to stop buying lettuce, they just have to stop buying lettuce from the affected source. That’s only possible if the industry can trace the product and give consumers accurate information, quickly and specifically enough to act on.
Recalling companies should be able to communicate quickly and clearly about which products were affected. Do they provide clear product identifiers so consumers can easily tell if the items they bought or consumed were part of the recall? Are messages simple to understand and act on? Is the company working collaboratively with their supply chain partners without pointing blame or becoming defensive? Are consumers hearing accurate, consistent information from both the supplier and the point where the product was sold?
Consumers are right to expect this level of communication. When the information doesn't come, people are left guessing about their own groceries, and that's not a position anyone should be in.
I can’t tell you that recalls are rare or that nothing has changed. Unfortunately, recalls are getting bigger and that’s a real problem the industry has to solve. But often, a recall means that the system caught a potentially harmful issue and is doing something about it. The companies that communicate well in the midst of the recall have the best chance of avoiding additional harm through the viral spread of inaccurate or incomplete information. People went looking for information about their food this summer and found a number on social media instead. The industry can do better than that, and should.
About the author:
Roger Hancock, CEO of
Recall InfoLink
, is an expert on recalls, with experience that spans the retail, tech, data, regulatory, and supply chain. Roger is also a steering committee member of the
Alliance for Recall Ready Communities
.

news_title: Stewart’s Shops Ice Cream Recalled For Metal Pieces - foodpoisoningbulletin.com
efet_title: Stewart’s Shops Ice Cream Recalled For Metal Pieces - foodpoisoningbulletin.com
efet_body:
Stewart’s Shops ice cream is being
recalled
in two flavors for possible foreign material contamination in the form of metal pieces. This poses a tooth injury, mouth injury, choking, and GI tract injury hazard. The recalling firm is Stewart’s Shops Corporation of Saratoga Springs, New York.
These products were sold at Stewart’s’ Shops locations in the states of New York, Vermont, and New Hampshire. They were for sale from July 17, 2026 to October 2, 2026. These ice cream products are ready to eat and intended to be consumed at home.
The recalled products include Heavenly Medley with a best by date of February 10, 2027. The shelf life of the product is 7 months. It is sold in one half gallon paperboard cartons. The UPC number that is stamped on the label is 0 82086 44371 1. Also recalled is Vanilla-Chocolate-Strawberry with a best by date of February 11, 2027. The shelf life of this product is also seven months. It was sold in a one half gallon paperboard carton. The UPC number for this product is 0 82086 44377 3.
The recall was triggered when a metal object was discovered by a consumer in one of the cartons. You can see more pictures of the recalled Stewart’s Shops ice cream products at the FDA web site.
If you bought these items, do not eat them. You can throw them away in a secure trash can after double bagging them so other people can’t see them, or you can take them back to the store where you purchased them for a full refund.

news_title: Recall of Great Value and Trader Joe’s Frozen Berries Expanded - foodpoisoningbulletin.com
efet_title: Recall of Great Value and Trader Joe’s Frozen Berries Expanded - foodpoisoningbulletin.com
efet_body:
The recall of Great Value and Trader Joe’s frozen berries has been
expanded
for possible E. coli contamination to include more products. Previous recalls were issued on July 3, 2026 and September 3, 2026. The Great Value berries, along with GreenWise blueberries sold at Publix stores, were linked to an
E. coli O145 outbreak
that sickened at least 17 people in two states: Georgia and Florida. The recalling firm is Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A., of San Carlos, Chile.
The outbreak was linked to GreenWise frozen blueberries, which were used to make the Great Value product, sold at Walmart stores, and the Trader Joe’s product. This is the first time the Trader Joe’s product has been mentioned and recalled.
The recalled Great Value products were shipped to Walmart stores in 30 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin, and West Virginia, along with Puerto Rico. Check your freezers for the these products.
The recalled Trader Joe’s product was shipped to Trader Joe’s stores in 26 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and Wisconsin, along with Washington, D.C.
The recalled products include Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend packed in 10 ounce plastic pouches. The mix includes strawberries, blackberries, and blueberries. The UPC number is 7874211226, the lot codes on the front of the package are 6 031 01 and 6 041 01, and the best if used by dates are January 21, 2028 and February 10, 2028.
Also recalled is Great Value Organic Blueberries, also packaged in 10 ounce plastic pouches. The UPC number is 7874211213, the lot codes are 6 019 01 and 6 040 01, and the best if used by dates are January 19, 2028; February 9, 2028, and June 12, 2028.
Finally, Trader Joe’s Organic Mixed Berry blend is recalled. It is packaged in 12 ounce plastic pouches. The UPC number is 00977654, the lot code on the back of the package is 6 051 01, and the best before date is February 20, 2028. You can see more pictures of the recalled products at the FDA web site.
This action is taken as a precautionary measure because the blueberries used in them were part of the recalled berries.
If you bought these products, do not eat them, even if you plan to cook them first because of the possibility of cross-contamination. You can throw the berries away in a secure trash can after double bagging them, or you can take them back to the place of purchase for a refund.
If you ate these berries, monitor your health for the symptoms of an
E. coli infection
for the next week. If you gave them to children to eat, monitor their health for hemolytic uremic syndrome (
HUS
), a type of kidney failure. If anyone gets sick, see a doctor.

efet_title: Home Grown Broccoli Seeds Recalled For Possible Salmonella - foodpoisoningbulletin.com
efet_body:
Home Grown broccoli seeds are being
recalled
for possible Salmonella contamination. These seeds were recalled when they were identified as being used by a sprout grower whose finished products were linked to a Salmonella outbreak, possibly the
Evergreen Sprouts outbreak
. No illnesses have been linked to this product to date. The recalling firm is EAK Distribution of Casper, Wyoming.
The recalled products include Home Grown Green Sprouting Calabrese Broccoli Seeds that are packaged in an 8 ounce package. These seeds were sold on Amazon to consumers nationwide between August 20, 2026 and September 18, 2026. Also recalled is the same product, also in an 8 ounce container which is a cream colored pouch with the UPC number 850056627443. The top seal is embossed with the production lot code AUG172026. The recall notice did not mention if this product was also sold on Amazon.
On September 16th EAK Distribution were notified by their seed supplier that there could be an issue with the original broccoli seed lot #W4105 that EAK Distribution had purchased. The seed supplier has recalled the affected seed bulk lot. On September 17th all sales were halted. EAK Distribution was notified by their supplier on September 28, 2026 that Salmonella bacteria was detected in the broccoli seed sample that was collected and analyzed the FDA. They have ceased all production and distribution of the affected product.
If you purchased these products, do not use them. You can throw the seeds away in a secure trash can after first double bagging them so others can’t see them, then you can contact Amazon for a refund.
If you ate these seeds or sprouted them and ate them, monitor your health for the
symptoms
of a Salmonella infection for the next week. If you do get sick, see your doctor.

news_title: Sprouting seeds recalled because of Salmonella risk
efet_title: Sprouting seeds recalled because of Salmonella risk
efet_body:
EAK Distribution of Casper, WY, is recalling Home Grown Green Sprouting Calabrese Broccoli Seeds, Heirloom, in 8-ounce packages because they have the potential to be contaminated with Salmonella.
Home Grown Green Sprouting Calabrese Broccoli Seeds Heirloom was sold on Amazon.com to consumers nationwide between Aug. 20 and Sept. 18.
The sprouting seeds are in a cream colored pouch with the UPC code 850056627443. The top seal is embossed with the Production Lot Code of AUG172026.
There have been no reported illnesses from our product to date.
The recall was initiated after the company’s seed supplier notified the company that the seeds were identified as being used by a sprout grower whose finished product were part of an FDA investigation involving a multi-state foodborne illness outbreak.
On Sept. 16 EAK Distribution was notified by our seed supplier that there could be an issue with the original broccoli seed lot #W4105 that EAK Distribution had purchased. Our seed supplier has recalled the affected seed bulk lot. On Sept. 17 all sales were halted. EAK Distribution was notified by our supplier on Sept. 28 that Salmonella was detected in the broccoli seed sample that was collected and analyzed the FDA. The company has ceased all production and distribution of the affected product.
About Salmonella infections
Food contaminated with Salmonella bacteria does not usually look, smell, or taste spoiled. Anyone can become sick with a Salmonella infection. Infants, children, seniors, and people with weakened immune systems are at higher risk of serious illness because their immune systems are fragile.
Anyone who has eaten any of the recalled product and developed symptoms of Salmonella infection should seek medical attention. Sick people should tell their doctors about the possible exposure to Salmonella bacteria because special tests are necessary to diagnose salmonellosis. Salmonella infection symptoms can mimic other illnesses, frequently leading to misdiagnosis.
Symptoms of Salmonella infection can include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever within 12 to 72 hours after eating contaminated food. Otherwise, healthy adults are usually sick for four to seven days. In some cases, however, diarrhea may be so severe that patients require hospitalization.
Older adults, children, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems, such as cancer patients, are more likely to develop a severe illness and serious, sometimes life-threatening conditions.
Some people get infected without getting sick or showing any symptoms. However, they may still spread the infections to others.

news_title: Bell & Evans announces $152 million expansion, upgrade for Pennsylvania facility - meat+poultry
efet_title: Bell & Evans announces $152 million expansion, upgrade for Pennsylvania facility - meat+poultry
efet_body:
HARRISBURG, PA. – Poultry producer Bell & Evans and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro recently confirmed a $152 million investment in an expansion at the company’s Bethel Township facility.
The project includes creating at least 380 jobs over the next three years and keeping more than 2,500 full-time positions.
The expansion of its Plant Two operation in Bethel Township includes a 50,000-square-foot addition to support further poultry processing and packaging.
“We’re proud to be leading the growth of Pennsylvania agriculture and appreciate the ongoing support from the Governor’s BusinessPA team, Secretary Redding and our local dignitaries,” said Scott Sechler, Sr., owner and chairman of Bell & Evans. “Pennsylvania is our home. We’re here to stay — building communities, creating strong livelihoods for our team members and offering stability for farmers.”
The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania plans to invest $2 million into Bell & Evans with the help of the Governor’s BusinessPA team and the Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED).
“Bell & Evans has been a part of Pennsylvania’s economy for more than a hundred years – and this investment will continue to support family farms and ensure we remain a national leader in the agriculture industry for generations to come,” Shapiro said. “Deals like this are proof that putting agriculture at the center of Pennsylvania’s economic development strategy is working.”
A fifth-generation family business, Bell & Evans is one of America’s oldest branded chicken operations. The company produces 100% all-natural Raised Without Antibiotics chicken and organic-certified products with no commodity production while maintaining the highest animal welfare standards in poultry.
Other agricultural state figures expressed their support for the project, including Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding and Pennsylvania Farm Bureau President Tommy Nagle, who praised the meaningful investment.

news_title: Fiber, flavor and function drive grocery innovation - meat+poultry
efet_title: Fiber, flavor and function drive grocery innovation - meat+poultry
efet_body:
DOWNERS GROVE, ILL. — Fiber enhanced products, globally inspired flavors and meals and functionality are among the trends Fresh Thyme Market expects to influence grocery innovation in 2027.
In partnership with SPINS, a provider of consumer packaged goods data, insights and commerce solutions, the companies highlighted what trends will be driving innovations in the annual Top 10 Trends report.
“The 2027 trends reflect a consumer who is informed, intentional and is looking for a basket of items that are innovative, curated, convenient and support their long-term well-being goals,” said Cecily Martinez, a registered dietitian at Fresh Thyme Market.
Fresh Thyme Market’s Top 10 Trends include:
Global flavor mashups are being inspired by global cuisine across the grocery store.
The brain food era will see more food and supplements positioned to support focus, memory and healthy aging.
Bite-size joys will feature curated assortments of premium snacks, mini desserts, specialty beverages and other small luxuries.
Fiber first will consist of more curated assortments of bread, cereals, snacks, beverages and everyday staples as consumers look to fiber as part of a broader approach to their overall wellness.
Sprinkle culture is all about customization for consumers. Fresh Thyme said it expects to see sauces, seasonings, crunchy toppings and other add-ons so consumers may have more control over the newest innovations in flavor, texture and nutrition.
More in every bite will include foods that deliver greater nutritional value in every serving to fit into consumers’ lifestyles. Fresh Thyme said products will combine protein, fiber, healthy fats and other nutrients.
Fresh from the fridge is driving consumers to the refrigerated aisles for fresh snacks that Fresh Thyme said will include protein bites, dips, chilled beverages and snackable produce.
Elevated meal shortcuts will entice consumers to look for what Fresh Thyme said are fresh marinated proteins, prepared vegetables, meal kits and ready-to-heat entrees.
The resourceful kitchen is expected to have products that extend freshness, reduce waste or work across multiple meals.
Frozen passport will showcase globally inspired meals, authentic flavors and high-quality solutions so international cuisines may be eaten at home.
The ocean pantry is a bonus trend that Fresh Thyme also identified as a growing trend where consumers are seeking seafood, seaweed snacks, kelp-based ingredients and algae-derived products.

news_title: Meat Institute marks 120 years of industry service - meat+poultry
efet_title: Meat Institute marks 120 years of industry service - meat+poultry
efet_body:
ARLINGTON, VA. – The month of October marks 12 decades of the Meat Institute’s service and representation for the meat and poultry industry. Several of the association’s members recognized the milestone 120
th
anniversary in a
celebratory video
.
“For 120 years, the Meat Institute has stood alongside the men and women who feed this country and the world,” said Julie Anna Potts, Meat Institute president and chief executive officer. “This anniversary is a celebration of their work — the packers, processors and suppliers who show up every day to sustainably nourish local and global communities with wholesome meat and poultry. I’m extremely proud to lead this organization into its next chapter, and grateful for the members who have carried it here.”
The Meat Institute was founded as the American Meat Packers Association in 1906 in Chicago after Congress passed the Federal Meat Inspection Act. At that time, the organization devoted its efforts to helping members adjust to the new federal inspection requirements and advocating for greater meat export opportunities and sponsoring early meat nutrition research.
Renamed the Institute of American Meat Packers 1919, and taking on the name the American Meat Institute (AMI) in 1940, it began to expand into consumer education, scientific research and industry promotion. AMI moved its headquarters to Washington, DC, in 1979 to be closer to federal policymakers as regulatory and legislative issues took on greater importance for the industry.
A merger with the North American Meat Association in 2015 brought the industry’s leading trade organizations together to form the North American Meat Institute (NAMI). NAMI offered one unified voice to speak to food safety, regulatory and policy issues. In 2024, the organization shortened its name to the Meat Institute as part of a broader rebrand.
Today, the Meat Institute provides regulatory guidance, advocacy before federal, state, local and international decision makers, market access, research and a community of industry peers to member packers, processors and suppliers across the country. The organization serves its members with a shared vision to sustainably nourish local and global communities with wholesome meat and poultry.
In celebration of the 120-year anniversary, the Meat Institute hosted the first-ever Meat Week in September. The event included a fly in, in which more than 40 member company representatives were brought to Capitol Hill to meet with lawmakers and administration officials and the second annual All-American Meat-Up at Nationals Park, celebrating the people and products behind American agriculture and animal protein.

news_title: Ribbonwire Ranch scales organic beef snack distribution - meat+poultry
efet_title: Ribbonwire Ranch scales organic beef snack distribution - meat+poultry
efet_body:
DALHART, TEXAS – Officials with Ribbonwire Ranch, announced the company is expanding its retail distribution of its organic beef snacks to more than 5,900 outlets across the country. Retail chains Kroger, Super 1 Foods, Albertsons, Gelson’s, Erewhon and Bashas are among the stores now carrying Ribbonwire’s 100% USDA Certified Organic Beef Sticks, which debuted in June and were already being sold at more than 800 Sheetz stores. The beef sticks are also available on Amazon and on the company’s website.
Promotion of the expansion included launching a redesigned Ribbonwire Ranch website in mid-September, which now features details on its products and the 140-year ranching story behind the brand. Ribbonwire offers four varieties of its meat snacks, including: Original, Sweet N’ Spicy, Honey BBQ and Jalapeno. The products are made with cattle born and raised on a certified organic farming operation and ranch in the panhandle of Texas.
“The response since June has exceeded our expectations,” said Chad Schoonover, Ribbonwire Ranch co-founder and head of ranch operations.
In the coming months, the company plans to promote the domestically raised and produced products with the US Department of Agriculture’s Product of USA label to highlight the company’s meat is from animals born, raised, slaughtered and processed in the United States.
“Everyone is paying attention to where their beef comes from now,” Schoonover said. “For Ribbonwire, that answer has always been clear. We raise our own cattle in Texas, grow our own organic feed and oversee the process from pasture to package.”
The Product of the USA promotion will roll out over the next six months and be featured on product packaging and highlighted on its social media platforms,
website
and Ribbonwire’s Amazon listing.

news_title: Ingredient Issues: The acceleration of bacon innovations - meat+poultry
efet_title: Ingredient Issues: The acceleration of bacon innovations - meat+poultry
efet_body:
Protein is currently one of the strongest drivers of food innovation. To differentiate, formulators are trying to deliver elevated sensory experiences. Bacon is proving to be an attractive food to meet today’s consumers’ cravings.
“Bacon continues to resonate with consumers because it sits at the intersection of two trends: the desire for high-protein foods and the desire for indulgence,” said Garrett McCoy, senior manager, research, development and applications, Corbion, Lenexa, Kan. “Bacon naturally checks both boxes because it offers familiarity, flavor and versatility across a wide range of applications.”
Premium is trending
Research from Innova Market Insights, The Netherlands, shows continued growth in premium, indulgent and texture-focused meat products. This creates opportunities for manufacturers to differentiate through both flavor and product format, as well as protein sources beyond pork.
“Whether it’s thicker-cut bacon, gourmet pork belly applications, chef-inspired seasoning blends or bacon snacks with more complex flavor layering, consumers increasingly view indulgence as more than just richness,” McCoy said. “They are looking for products that deliver texture, aroma, flavor complexity and an overall eating experience that feels worth the purchase.”
Sidney Brommel, marketing communications research analyst, Kemin Food Technologies, Des Moines, Iowa, said, “Smoke differentiation is being perceived as a premiumization. We see applewood, cherrywood, pecan-smoked, oak-aged smoke and whiskey barrel-smoked as a selling point for premium bacon products.
“There also is a big surge in various limited-time-offering flavor concepts for bacon,” Brommel added. “Just about every major player in the space has offered some new flavors over the past few years.”
Limited-edition Wright Brand Hot Honey Flavored Real Wood Smoked Thick Cut Bacon from Tyson Foods, Springdale, Ark., is a thick-cut pork bacon with a sweet-heat flavor profile. It includes subtle notes of red pepper and vinegar, balanced with honey, garlic and onion.
Hormel Black Label Frank’s RedHot flavored bacon was a recent co-branded limited-time-offering from Hormel Foods, Austin, Minn. These premium thick-cut slices featured a smoke and spice flavor profile.
Convenience complements premiumization. Hatfield, part of family-owned Clemens Food Group, Hatfield, Pa., now offers a fully cooked bacon topping for foodservice. The product is designed to assist short-staffed operators with being more efficient. There’s no raw handling, no cook time and no skilled labor required.
“This clever hack helps operators do more with less,” said Jenny Moyer Murphy, corporate executive chef at Clemens Food Group, Hatfield, Pa. “It opens the door for effortless experimentation with innovative applications — from savory salads to on-trend ‘swavory’ desserts — all without adding extra work to already busy teams. It’s about delivering that essential bacon flavor and texture, efficiently, consistently and deliciously.”
Bacon offers procesors a familiar platform for experimentation and innovation.
|
Source: Donna Berry
Zak Otto, director of protein research and development, R&D, Wixon, St. Francis, Wis., said, “Alternative bacon meat, such as turkey and beef, has become a little more mainstream as well.”
Niman Ranch, Westminster, Colo., recently introduced 100% Grass-Fed and Grass-Finished Beef Bacon. It is pit-smoked and dry-rubbed, which provides a rich, complex flavor profile, according to the company.
“By using the navel, the beef equivalent of pork belly, we’ve achieved that elusive balance of melt-in-your-mouth fat and satisfying chew that bacon lovers crave,” said Andrew Hunter, Niman Ranch’s executive chef.
Bacon jerky remains an underdeveloped meat snack sector. That is likely to change.
“You can go well beyond just smoked or sweet flavors in jerky. Even global flavors could be used,” Otto said. “Flavor combinations like mango habanero or spicy teriyaki can be applied to give a brand a signature flavor. With these various flavor combinations, bacon jerky could be thought of outside of the breakfast daypart, fitting into any time of day.”
Brommel said, “Bacon also has the benefit of being considered keto-friendly. Bacon jerky could lean into the growing protein, meat snack trend and could be flexible in marketing to different lifestyles and diets.”
Pork bacon jerky, compared to other meat jerkies, is highly prone to lipid oxidation. This can lead to the development of rancid flavors.
“It is highly vulnerable as it combines high-fat content, protein, oxygen exposure and extended shelf-life expectations,” Brommel said. “Antioxidant systems should be considered early in bacon jerky development because antioxidants can help stabilize smoke flavor, spice and flavor systems, fat quality and consumer-perceived freshness.”

Gias Foods, Inc., is expanding a previous recall to now include every lot code of Bettergoods brand Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine over fears the product could be contaminated with listeria, an alert from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Thursday.
The frozen recalled pasta was distributed across the country to Walmart stores. All lot code numbers are now being recalled, and the product is packaged in 22-ounce yellow plastic, with a UPC number of 194346442706.
There have been no reported illnesses related to the recalled pasta, the alert says.
Read More
on
News
Numerous recalls have been issued this year across the country due to the potential for damage, foodborne illness, contamination, lack of inspection or undeclared food allergens. Recently, federal officials also announced a recent recall from Star Meat Delivery Inc. impacting about 167,639 pounds of
raw beef, pork and goat
because the goods were produced without federal inspection.
When reached by
Newsweek
for comment, a communications representative for Walmart said, "Safety is a top priority. When notified of recalls, we move quickly to remove the impacted products from our stores and implement a sales block at registers and online. We are working closely with our supplier, and customers who have this should discontinue use and follow the recall instructions."
Newsweek
reached out to Gias Foods, Inc., via email Friday for additional information.
...
What To Know About the Recall
According to the alert,
the recall followed routine sampling by both the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, which flagged that the finished product could contain the bacteria.
"The company has ceased the distribution of the product as FDA and the company continue their investigation as to what caused the problem," the alert added.
Last month, the product was given
a Class I designation. The FDA describes Class I as "a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death."
People who have purchased the recalled frozen pasta are urged to return it to the original place of purchase for a refund. Consumers with additional questions may contact the company via email at
sales@giasfoods.com
, the alert says.
The FDA warns that
Listeria monocytogenes
is an organism that could potentially cause serious and sometimes fatal infections in people with weakened immune systems, those who are frail or older adults, and children. It could also cause miscarriages or stillbirths in pregnant women and short-term symptoms for healthy people could include high fever, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, severe headache and stiffness.
Recall Concerns and Foodborne Illness in 2026
The latest recall update impacting the frozen pasta comes amid heightened fears and attention to foodborne illnesses and recalls,
including national cases of salmonella
and
cyclospora.
The largest case involving cyclospora this year was in connection with iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) announced
last month that the outbreak was over
after thousands were sickened nationwide.
Similarly, a recall of fresh jalapenos over salmonella concerns prompted additional recalls impacting dips, salsas and other prepared foods. As of Friday, nearly 500 people have been reported sick and 65 hospitalized,
according to the FDA.
Keith Schneider, professor of food safety at the UF Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, said in a release sent to
Newsweek
last month when asked why some recalls involve very large companies or well-known grocery stores, "Large companies distribute enormous amounts of food, so problems involving those products are more likely to be detected."
Schneider added, "Imagine one supplier distributes a million units of a product. If there is a contamination problem, there is a much greater chance that multiple people will become sick and that health officials will see a pattern. A small farm selling a few dozen units may have the same contamination rate, but if only one person becomes sick, that illness may never be connected to the farm or producer. That doesn't mean a large food company is necessarily less safe. Sometimes it simply means the scale of its distribution makes a problem easier to see."

A $500 ratification bonus

Improved short-term disability coverage
Expanded insurance benefits
Wendell W. Young, president of the UFCW Local 1776, also congratulated the workers at Cargill Hazelton on reaching the agreement.
“At a time when the beef industry is facing significant challenges, this contract represents meaningful progress for the membership and reflects the value of having a strong union at the bargaining table,” Young said.

DUCHESNE, UTAH – Farm Creek Meats, a family owned and operated meat processing facility in Duchesne, Utah, received a $200,000
Value-added Producer Grant
from US Department of Agriculture Rural Development.
The grant will help Farm Creek Meats expand its customer base and strengthen its retail presence to increase overall sales, the agency said. The working capital funds will be used to broaden product offerings, support production capacity and enter new markets. Additionally, the investment will also enhance Farm Creek’s ability to meet growing demand of locally raised and processed meat products, improve operational stability and position the company for long‑term growth and profitability.
“We are extremely grateful to USDA Rural Development for selecting Farm Creek Meats for this Value-Added Producer Grant,” said Douglas Reid, Farm Creek Meats owner. “As a producer-owned, vertically integrated meat company in rural Utah, this award gives us the opportunity to take what we raise and produce here at home and create higher-value products that can compete on a national level.
“This funding will help us bring innovative products like our 100% bison and elk sticks to more consumers, expand markets for our products, and create additional opportunities for agriculture and rural communities,” Reid added. “We appreciate USDA’s investment in small producers and rural businesses like ours, and we’re excited about what this grant will help us build.”
Source: US Department of Agriculture
USDA Rural Development’s Value-Added Producer Grant Program helps producers develop value-added agricultural products, conduct market research and implement business and marketing strategies. Applications for the Value-Added Producer Grant program are typically accepted for processing from agricultural producers between January and May, depending on when program funding is allocated, the agency said.
“Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins is highly focused on supporting American farmers and locally raised food products,” said Rural Development Utah State Director Stan Summers. “Farm Creek Meats is a great example of Utah producers strengthening our agricultural economy and supporting our nation’s goals. This investment will give the company the backing it needs to expand its reach, bring more locally raised products to market, and set themselves up for long‑term opportunities.”

news_title: Stoney Point Premium Snacks builds on butchering legacy - meat+poultry
efet_title: Stoney Point Premium Snacks builds on butchering legacy - meat+poultry
efet_body:
Evan Arndt, owner of Stoney Point Premium Snacks, Littlestown, Pa., carries four generations of butchers’ blood. Arndt’s great grandfather began the legacy by starting a butcher shop in the Pennsylvania borough of East Berlin. There were two sons, Wayne and Evan Arndts’s grandfather, Charlie Nell, who carried on the trade and started another butcher shop as partners in the mid-1950s. The Nell brothers split and in 1980 Arndt’s grandfather moved to Littlestown to start his own shop that became Stoney Point Farm Market. Arndt’s mother, Michelle, worked in the shop, then in 1986 his father, Bruce Arndt, began work at the shop.
“So, I literally grew up in a butcher shop more or less the whole way through,” Arndt said. “I grew up working on the kill floor, trimming, doing deer processing. So, the butchering end of it was always in my blood.”
In 1997, Arndt’s grandparents sold the butcher shop, Arndt was 13 years old with a sister two years older. Arndt’s parents stayed on and worked for the new owner for roughly seven years. The new ownership took the business in the direction of lower cost, cheaper product in greater quantity, rather than the high-quality the family had sold in the past.
“We had a retail store in the front and processing in the back,” Arndt said. “And over those seven years is when my dad got very tired of working for somebody that he saw ruining the company, bringing the company down.”
In April 2000, Bruce Arndt took a pivotal step that changed everything. He read the entrepreneurial and personal finance classic, “Rich Dad Poor Dad: What the Rich Teach Their Kids About Money that the Poor and Middle Class Do Not!” by Robert Kiyosaki. Then he gave the book to Evan, and he read it.
“I was 14, something like that at that point,” Arndt said. “He gave me the book and said, ‘listen, I am tired of working for somebody else and for other people’s dreams. I really want to start something with the family.’ And from there, it morphed within about six months.”
Evan Arndt's grandparents started the original butcher shop in Littlestown in 1980. (Source: Stoney Point Premium Snacks)
New chapter
While Bruce and Michelle Arndt still worked at the original butcher shop for the new ownership in 2001, they managed to buy a jerky shop from a gentleman named Earl who brought jerky under the brand of Stoney Point Jerky into the butcher shop and sold it out of a jar at the retail counter. Then in 2004, they were able to purchase the original butcher shop, and the family business came to fruition.
“By 2004, the gentleman that owned the butcher shop could not make payments anymore on the property,” Arndt said. “And my grandma, being the business savvy person that she was, held the whole entire note of the building. So on April Fool’s Day, 2004, we [Bruce and Michelle Arndt] ended up buying the butcher shop from my grandma after the other gentleman had lost it.”
By 2020, The Stoney Point Farm Market, the butcher shop and retail store, and Stoney Point Premium Snacks, the jerky business, split into separate businesses. Evan took over the jerky business, and his sister took the butcher shop and market. It all happened in tandem with COVID and Arndt had a gut feeling about what was ahead for the market.
“I was coming back from Cincinnati, and I remember vividly watching the TV screen and it was going over COVID and what it was going to do to different markets,” he said. “They said the beef market’s going to drop because no restaurants are going to be open. I remember calling my dad and I said, ‘Hey, I’m going to go ahead and buy out three to four months’ worth of meat. I honestly think the price is going to go up, not down.’ We bought that product and it was no later than about six weeks and everything went through the absolute rooftops from $3.50 to $6, or more. We had product to produce.”
The purchase put Stoney Point Premium in a position to provide product when other processors cut back or stopped altogether. Stoney Point Premium and Sheetz, the Mid-Atlantic gas and convenience chain, agreed on a large contract. Stoney Point’s Bronco Billy brand, purchased in the early 2010s from the Curry family, began to grow rapidly. Stoney Point’s products then ended up in Wawa and Rutter’s convenience chains.
“I want to say 2019, we were doing maybe right around $3 million, and then that kind of breaks us into the $6 million, $7 million mark,” Arndt said. “So, this year, we’re looking at $15 million with what we’re taking on. We should be hitting $20 million or more going into next year.”
With that type of business growth comes the need for physical facility capability growth. In 2001, Stoney Point Premium’s original jerky facility was approximately 100 square feet. The Arndts rebuilt the family garage taking it from 300 square feet to 1,100 square feet for jerky production.
In roughly 2008, a building a short distance from the butcher shop became available through the Arndt’s accountant. The family had interest but didn’t want to…[truncated]

MCLEAN, VA. — The Food Production Solutions Association (FPSA) will host Cultivate: Leadership Growth Lab on November 5-6, 2026, in Lexington, Ky., bringing together early- to mid-career professionals from across the food and beverage industry for two days of hands-on leadership development, peer learning, and real-world application.
Unlike traditional leadership conferences built around presentations and lectures, Cultivate is designed as an immersive experience where participants actively practice leadership skills through simulations, facilitated discussions, team challenges, site observations, and personal reflection.
The experience begins before attendees even arrive, with a complimentary DiSC® assessment that helps participants better understand their communication style, leadership tendencies, and how they interact with others. Throughout the event, self-awareness becomes the foundation for a series of interactive leadership experiences designed to strengthen communication, influence, decision-making, collaboration, and confidence.
"Leadership isn't developed by sitting in a room and listening to someone talk about it," said Chris Lyons, President & CEO of FPSA. "Cultivate gives participants the opportunity to practice leadership, receive feedback, learn from peers, and see it in action. They will leave with tools they can immediately apply in their careers."
According to FPSA's workforce research, leadership and problem-solving skills remain among the areas organizations struggle most to develop. Cultivate was created to help address that need through practical, experience-based learning.
A Leadership Journey, Not a Conference
Over two days, participants will:
Complete a complimentary DiSC® assessment and explore how their communication style impacts leadership effectiveness
Join a small Cultivate Circle that serves as a peer learning and accountability group throughout the program
Participate in interactive leadership simulations requiring communication, collaboration, and decision-making under pressure
Practice navigating difficult workplace conversations and providing constructive feedback
Learn how to build influence and gain buy-in without relying on title or authority
Observe leadership, teamwork, and operational excellence in action during a visit to the Toyota Kentucky Experience Center
Work through real-world leadership challenges with peers and industry facilitators
Create a personal leadership action plan to apply immediately after returning to work
Throughout the program, participants will learn from a diverse group of entrepreneurs, executive coaches, leadership experts, and industry professionals, including Jason Burke, Founder of New Primal, Emma Hossack, Amy Goodson, Leslie Minchin, Donald Woolridge, and John Parke.
A highlight of the experience includes an evening reception and networking event at RD1 Distillery, where participants can continue conversations, strengthen professional relationships, and Hear from RD1's Master Distiller about how he innovates and brings new products to market.
Designed for the Next Generation of Industry Leaders
Cultivate was developed for professionals who are beginning to lead projects, influence teams, supervise others, or prepare for expanded leadership responsibilities. The program focuses on practical skills participants can use immediately, helping them become stronger communicators, more confident decision-makers, and more effective leaders.
"The goal is simple," Lyons said. "We want participants to leave with greater self-awareness, stronger leadership skills, and a network of peers they can continue learning from long after the event ends."
Sponsorship and Registration Information
Organizations looking to support the development of emerging leaders while increasing their visibility within the food and beverage industry can explore a variety of Cultivate sponsorship opportunities. Sponsorship packages are designed to create meaningful engagement with attendees before, during, and after the event.
With less than five weeks until Cultivate, FPSA encourages organizations and individuals to secure their spot for this immersive leadership development experience. A special Send Three, Pay for Two registration offer is available for teams looking to invest in the next generation of leaders.
The hotel reservation deadline is October 11, 2026, and registration closes October 30, 2026. Additional information and registration details are available at fpsa.org/cultivate.

CHICAGO — Conagra Brands Inc. is executing on its plan to shore up its financial performance and has begun a portfolio review, president and chief executive officer John Brase said in reporting improved bottom- and top-line results for the fiscal 2027 first quarter.
“After spending the quarter working closely with our teams and engaging across the organization, I’m even more confident that we’re focused on the right opportunities and taking the right actions,” said Brase, who
became Conagra’s CEO
on June 1. “We delivered a solid start to the fiscal year, despite a challenging operating environment. But, overall, we feel good about our execution thus far.
“We’re making tangible progress against the priorities
we laid out last quarter
. It’s still early, but we’re moving from words to action. And we’re already seeing encouraging proof points.”
For the first quarter ended Aug. 24, net income rose 6% to $174.3 million, equal to 36¢ per share on the common stock, from $164.5 million, or 34¢ per share, a year earlier. Adjusted net earnings edged up 4.3% to $197.3 million, or 41¢ per share, from $189.2 million, or 39¢ per share, a year ago. Conagra attributed the uptick mainly to lower adjusted SG&A expenses and higher equity earnings. The adjusted earnings-per-share result beat analysts’ high-end average estimate of 32¢.
Net sales dipped 1.4% to $2.6 billion from $2.63 billion, compared with a 6% year-over-year decline a year ago. Conagra said the decrease in the fiscal 2027 quarter reflected a 0.5% negative impact from divested businesses, a 0.2% increase from foreign exchange and a 1.1% downtick in organic net sales. Organic sales included a 2.1% decrease in volume and a 1% gain in price/mix.

Please check to see if you have this item in your establishment. If you do, do not eat it, serve it, or sell it to others.
You can throw the sausages away in a secure trash bin after first double bagging them so other people can’t see them, or you can contact your distributor to arrange a return and a refund.

G. L. Mezzetta Inc. is voluntarily recalling a certain lot number of Mezzetta GOLDEN GREEK PEPERONCINI MEDIUM HEAT, 32-ounce, due to concerns of a potential pest contaminant in the jar, an alert from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said.
"We’re aware of a video circulating on social media showing a potential pest contaminant in a jar of Mezzetta GOLDEN GREEK PEPERONCINI MEDIUM HEAT, 32-ounce. We have contacted the consumer and have moved quickly to investigate the situation and initiate a voluntary recall," the alert said in part.
A video posted to TikTok circulated earlier this month and now has over 230,000 views shows what appears to be a rodent floating in the jar of peppers. "Here with the pot roast I wanted to make, Mississippi style, but there's a dead baby mouse, there's a dead baby mouse in my pepperoncini's," a woman in the video says in part.
Read More
on
News
There have been no reported illnesses or injuries related to the recall, the alert notes. No other products are included in the recall.
Newsweek
reached out to G. L. Mezzetta Inc. via email on Monday night for comment.
...
What To Know
According to the alert,
the recall only impacts GOLDEN GREEK PEPERONCINI MEDIUM HEAT, 32 oz., with a lot number of 720106 and SKU number of 10106328. The alert says the company has identified where the recalled product was distributed and the customers who received the product.
The alert says the company is "working directly with them to isolate and remove the affected product from sale."
The product referenced in the original consumer report has been requested to be retrieved and analyzed to review sanitation and food safety records as well as the relevant production, the alert says.
People who have purchased the recalled peppers are urged not to consume them and to contact the company via email at CustomerSupport@Mezzetta.com.
Numerous recalls have been issued this year across the country due to the potential for damage, foodborne illness, contamination, lack of inspection or undeclared food allergens. Recently, federal officials also announced a recent recall from Star Meat Delivery Inc. impacting about 167,639 pounds of
raw beef, pork and goat
because the goods were produced without federal inspection.
The latest recall impacting the jarred peperoncini comes amid heightened fears and attention to foodborne illnesses and recalls,
including national cases of salmonella
and
cyclospora.
Keith Schneider, professor of food safety at the UF Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, said in a release sent to
Newsweek
earlier this month when asked if the number of food recalls and foodborne outbreaks taking place
recently has increased from past numbers, "Not necessarily."
"We tend to hear about them much more often because we have much greater access to information. We now have 24-hour news and social media, so when there is an outbreak or recall, people can hear about it repeatedly throughout the day. An actual news report can go viral, but so can information from someone who may not understand food safety or the science behind an outbreak," Schneider said.
"That can make it feel like we are seeing an unprecedented number of outbreaks when, in reality, many of the same foodborne pathogens and types of outbreaks have occurred for years. The reality is that we get an estimated 1.2 million cases of salmonella every year, which averages about 100,000 cases a month. There are about 20 million cases of norovirus each year. So, the numbers we’re seeing this summer are not out of the ordinary. The large number of cyclospora cases is unusually high for that organism. On average, we typically see 1,000 to 2,000 cases each year, so more than 20,000 cases is concerning," he added.

CARLSTADT, NJ. — Schweid & Sons, a family-owned and operated purveyor of premium protein, launched Marinated Steak Tips as an easy-prep product for consumers looking for chef-inspired flavors.
“Schweid & Sons has always believed that convenience should never come at the expense of quality,” said Jennifer Versacci, chief commercial officer at Schweid & Sons. “Our Marinated Steak Tips reflect that commitment by combining whole cuts of premium Tri-Tip with chef-inspired flavors and ready-to-cook convenience. We want consumers to spend less time prepping and more time enjoying great food with the people gathered around their table.”
Available in two varieties, Cajun Style and Teriyaki Style, the Marinated Steak Tips are made from whole cuts of Tri-Tip, ultra trimmed and hand butchered for quality. Marinated for an elevated taste experience without extra shopping or seasoning, the steak tips offer bold flavor and are conveniently packaged for freshness.
Schweid & Sons said Cajun Style and Teriyaki Style are two of the most sought-after flavor profiles. Teriyaki delivers sweet, savory depth, while the Cajun marinade embeds bold spice into the beef cuts.
Ready within minutes, the Marinated Steak Tips can be cooked straight from the package for a quick and versatile dinner solution. The product is perfect for steakhouse-inspired plates, rice bowls, tacos, skewers, sandwiches, salads, stir-fries or simply high-protein snacks, said Schweid & Sons.
Marinated Steak Tips’ debut builds on Schweid & Sons’ growing portfolio of craft, premium beef as the company seeks to expand into new meal occasions for modern consumers.
